implementation_notes: Rails ships the pattern as CurrentAttributes: a Current class declares attribute :account, :user, and every layer of the request reads Current.user without a parameter, because the store is a thread-isolated singleton that the framework resets before and after each request (reset is part of the request cycle, and resets { } hooks clean up dependent state). Rack's env hash is the explicit alternative - middleware and endpoints receive the request and pass what they need - and outside Rails a plain thread-local or an explicitly threaded value object is the manual fallback. The Rails documentation itself warns against overuse: Current is for a few top-level globals shared by all actions, not a dumping ground for controller-specific data.
code_sketch:
class Current < ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes
  attribute :account, :user, :request_id
end

# before_action at the boundary
Current.user = authenticated_user
Current.request_id = request.uuid

# anywhere below - models, services, jobs
Current.account.messages.create(message_params)
pitfalls: CurrentAttributes is thread-isolated, not fiber-isolated: under a fiber-based scheduler running many requests on one thread, concurrent requests can share the same Current instance.

It is a global singleton whose lifetime is the request cycle it wraps - work handed to a background job or an after-commit callback sees whatever Current happens to hold there, not the value from the request.
